newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, EU say strong ties key to Europe security.
newsitem.headline: Russia, EU say strong ties key to Europe security.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin told top representatives of the European Union on Monday that stronger ties between Russia and the 15-nation bloc were vital to continental security.

The EU delegation, including European Commission President Jacques Santer and Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, praised Russia's market reforms at talks in the Kremlin and vowed to help Russia become fully integrated into the world economy.

"Relations based on partnership and cooperation between Russia and the European Union are the key to strengthening security and stability on the continent," Yeltsin's press service said in a statement issued after the talks.
The statement said a previously agreed partnership and cooperation accord, designed to forge commercial links and to liberalise trade, would come into effect before the summer.
It added that agreement was reached in principle on a permanent mechanism to deal with economic, trade, scientific and cultural issues between Russia and the EU.
"It is clear that Russia and the European Union need each other and have the political will to cooperate," Kok told a news conference. The Netherlands currently holds the EU's rotating presidency.

Kok said the EU's talks with Yeltsin and Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin took place in "a very good atmosphere". He added that he had congratulated the Russian leadership for persevering with painful economic reforms.
"Of course problems remain but Russia is on the right track," Kok said.
He said the EU was helping Russia's reforms through a range of aid programmes and that Brussels would support Russia's bid to join the World Trade Organisation.

Yeltsin's EU summit was originally scheduled for February 4 in The Hague but had to be postponed when the president came down with pneumonia in January after a brief return to the Kremlin following his heart bypass operation last November.
On Monday Yeltsin was "in excellent spirits, a creative, active negotiating partner," Kok said.
Santer said the EU accounted for 40 percent of Russia's foreign trade, considerably more than the United States, but added there was ample scope for improvements.
Russia pressed claims for more access to European markets -- something EU companies fear could unleash a flood of cheap imports.
Kok said Yeltsin had repeated Moscow's fierce opposition to NATO's plans to admit former Soviet-bloc states in central and eastern Europe to the Atlantic alliance.

While noting that NATO and the EU are separate organisations, Kok said he believed Russia and the defence alliance would reach a compromise agreement before a Madrid summit in July when NATO will invite new members to join.

"The Russian attitude has not changed (from opposing NATO expansion) but at the same time there is a strong will to reach a set of conclusions before Madrid," said Kok, whose country also belongs to NATO.
Russia regards NATO's eastward enlargement as a threat to its own security and is seeking a legally binding treaty with the alliance safeguarding its interests.

Kok and Santer said Moscow had never expressed similar opposition to the EU's plans to expand eastwards. Most former communist countries in eastern Europe have associate EU membership, seen as a prelude to full membership.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted Yeltsin as telling his visitors: "We are satisfied that the European Union is developing and that you are getting more integration."
